claims.text: Untreated stainless steel has a native passive oxide film.
The native passive oxide film is insufficient to protect stainless steel in extreme corrosive environments.
A thin, dense TiN coating can be deposited on stainless steel by physical vapor deposition.
An in situ high-temperature electrochemical and microscopic measurement system can monitor TiN coating degradation and microstructural changes in real time.
High acidity, elevated temperature, or strongly oxidative conditions rapidly degrade conventional stainless steel surfaces.
A PVD-deposited TiN coating forms a chemically inert barrier over stainless steel.
A PVD-deposited TiN coating forms a low-permeability barrier over stainless steel.
The TiN barrier inhibits ingress of aggressive ions responsible for corrosion.
Real-time measurements of coating degradation can be used to fine-tune PVD deposition parameters.
Fine-tuning the deposition parameters using in situ feedback improves TiN coating density and adhesion.
Improved TiN coating density and adhesion enhance the corrosion resistance of stainless steel.
Stainless steel bearing an in situ-optimized TiN coating will have a substantially lower corrosion rate under extreme corrosive conditions than untreated stainless steel.
Microstructural indicators of TiN coating degradation will correlate clearly with electrochemical performance.
Correlations between degradation indicators and electrochemical performance can facilitate further improvements in coating quality.
The relative benefit of this approach in mild corrosive conditions is not assessed.
The accuracy of in situ feedback may depend on coating thickness and substrate preparation.
The magnitude of corrosion-resistance improvement is uncertain because relating in situ degradation indicators to long-term extreme-environment performance is challenging.
The sensitivity of the measurement system to subtle TiN microstructural defects requires further validation.
